sources.summary: Lucia co-owns Casa Verde, a 52-seat dinner-only trattoria doing ~110 covers on Saturdays, and has paid for BookBistro Pro for two years. Her biggest issues are reliability (double-bookings, silently broken reminders, slow support), manually typing DM and WhatsApp bookings, and metered SMS that turns $79 into ~$120. She is strongly pro-deposit for groups of six or more but would never charge a couple, and would only consider switching in January.

Tomasz owns Kettle & Crumb, a 22-seat café whose Thursday–Saturday set-menu supper is the only part that takes bookings, mostly over WhatsApp into a paper book. He sees little problem (10–15 minutes a day, ~3% no-shows), cancelled a SeatNow trial at $49/month, would consider $15–20, and rejects deposits, paid SMS and apps. His one real pain is writing a booking on the wrong page.

Oksana is the host at Sunny Side, a 64-seat brunch café where about 85% of 140–150 weekend covers are walk-ins managed on a clipboard. Her core pains are walk-aways, empty tables and endlessly answering how long the wait is; she loved a free QR-style queue tool (QueueBee) until the owner dropped it when it became paid. She wants guest self-sign-up by QR, SMS table-ready messages she'd happily pay per message for, table status from servers, and deposits only for groups of eight or more.

Devon runs the floor and front-of-house schedule at Harbor & Pine, a 90-seat seafood restaurant on SeatNow (~$129/month). SMS reminders halved no-shows and he'd happily pay more per text; a refundable $10/head prime-slot deposit pilot cut no-shows from 8% to under 2%. His open pains are phone volume, Sunday staffing guesswork, messy notes that hide allergies and guessed overbooking; he leans link-first but would test a guest app.

Priya eats out 4–5 times a month, finds places on Instagram and books by DM because she won't call; she switches restaurants about twice a month when calling is the only option. She wants a no-account link in the bio, a clear confirmation and a cancel link, prefers DM/WhatsApp to SMS, and finds deposits on ordinary dinners insulting. Recognition is only a bonus for her.

Marcus dines out about eight times a month at ~$70 a head and rotates three local favourites. Being known (his table, his partner's nut allergy) is why he returns; at a place that treats him as a stranger after ~30 visits he has quietly cut visits from monthly to quarterly. He wants a self-updated guest profile, would use an app only for places he visits often, is happy with SMS, and supports prime-slot deposits that are refundable, off the bill and waived for regulars.

nuggets.text: Lucia has paid $79/month for BookBistro's Pro plan for two years and is not happy with it.
nuggets.quote: BookBistro. Two years now. I pay seventy-nine dollars a month for the, uh, the Pro plan. And honestly, I'm not happy.

nuggets.text: Phone and online bookings collide because BookBistro's table map doesn't refresh, double-booking a table once or twice a month.
nuggets.quote: somebody else is booking online at the same moment, and the table map doesn't refresh. So I get two parties on table twelve. Maybe once or twice a month.

nuggets.text: BookBistro doesn't integrate with the Square POS, so the host tracks seated, paid and turning tables on a sticky note.
nuggets.quote: it doesn't talk to Square. We have Square for the POS. So I can't see who is seated, who paid, whether a table is turning. My host writes it on a sticky note.

nuggets.text: Lucia spends 25–30 minutes a day fixing the book (moving people, merging duplicates) and her host another ~20 minutes during service.
nuggets.quote: Twenty-five, thirty minutes a day just fixing the book. Moving people, merging duplicates, checking the table map against what is really happening. My host maybe another twenty during service.

nuggets.text: BookBistro's reminder emails silently stopped for about eight days last March and a human support ticket took three days to answer.
nuggets.quote: Last March the reminder emails stopped going out for, like, eight days and I only noticed because the no-shows went up. It took them three days to answer a human ticket.

nuggets.text: No-shows run about 9% with reminders and rose to about 15% when reminders broke, so reminders must be reliable.
nuggets.quote: With reminders, around nine percent. Without, when the emails broke, it was closer to fifteen. So I know the reminders work. I just don't trust the tool to send them.

nuggets.text: About 40% of bookings come by phone and 35% through the website widget, the rest via Instagram messages, WhatsApp and walk-ins.
nuggets.quote: Phone, still the biggest. Like forty percent. The website widget, maybe thirty-five. Then Instagram messages, WhatsApp, and walk-ins.

nuggets.text: Every evening Lucia manually types around 15 Instagram and WhatsApp booking messages into BookBistro, her least favourite job.
nuggets.quote: Every evening, yes. Around, I don't know, fifteen messages. It is my least favourite job.

nuggets.text: Lucia wants turn times learned from history (about 90 minutes on a Tuesday, 2.5 hours on a Saturday) instead of a fixed two-hour booking.
nuggets.quote: Second, show me when a table will actually be free. Not "this booking is two hours." People take ninety minutes on a Tuesday and two and a half on a Saturday with the dessert wine. I want it to learn that.

nuggets.text: Casa Verde takes a $15-per-head deposit only for parties of six or more on Fridays and Saturdays.
nuggets.quote: We use it only for parties of six or more, fifteen dollars per head, on Fridays and Saturdays.

nuggets.text: Before deposits, an 11-person table no-showed on a Saturday and cost about $600 in sales.
nuggets.quote: We lost a whole long table once, eleven people, on a Saturday. That was maybe six hundred dollars of sales gone.

nuggets.text: Since deposits, large-party no-shows fell from about one in four to almost never, so Lucia is strongly pro-deposit for groups.
nuggets.quote: But the large groups now show up, the no-show for big parties went from, like, one in four to almost never. So for groups I'm very pro.

nuggets.text: Lucia would never charge a deposit to a couple because they would just go next door.
nuggets.quote: For two people? No way. I would never charge a couple. They'd just go next door.

nuggets.text: Some guests complain about Casa Verde's group deposit, saying it is a trattoria, not a theatre.
nuggets.quote: Some complain. Some say "you're a trattoria, not a theatre."

nuggets.text: BookBistro includes 300 texts a month then charges 7 cents each; at ~900 texts Lucia pays ~$40 extra, so $79 is really ~$120.
nuggets.quote: The plan includes three hundred texts a month. After that, seven cents each. I send maybe nine hundred, so I pay another forty dollars or so.

nuggets.text: Per-message SMS pricing makes Lucia send fewer reminders, which brings no-shows back.
nuggets.quote: If a tool charges me per message I will send fewer, and then the no-shows come back. That's a bad incentive.

nuggets.text: Lucia would pay $89–90 a month all-in with unlimited SMS and no double-bookings, but not $79 plus metered texts, and would switch for that.
nuggets.quote: I would pay eighty-nine, ninety all in, if I never had the double-bookings and the SMS were unlimited. But not seventy-nine plus metered. I'd switch for that.

nuggets.text: Switching is blocked by two years of guest history (phone numbers, allergy notes) in a BookBistro CSV export with wrong columns.
nuggets.quote: Moving the data. Two years of guest history, the phone numbers, the notes about allergies. BookBistro lets me export a CSV but it's a mess, the columns are wrong.

nuggets.text: Retraining 12 staff before the holiday season is out; Lucia would only consider switching in January, her dead month.
nuggets.quote: January. January is dead. If you came in January, I'd listen.

nuggets.text: Lucia says nobody downloads an app for one trattoria; her guests aged 40–70 want to press a link or call.
nuggets.quote: Nobody downloads an app for one trattoria. My guests are, you know, from forty to seventy, they want to press a link and be done.

nuggets.text: A booking link on the Google listing and the Instagram bio covers about 90% of what Casa Verde needs online.
nuggets.quote: Honestly a link in the Google listing and in the Instagram bio is ninety percent of it.

nuggets.text: BookBistro's Google booking button sometimes shows 'no availability' when tables are free, losing bookings she only notices by accident.
nuggets.quote: BookBistro's button there sometimes shows "no availability" when we have tables, because the settings are confusing. I lose bookings and I only notice by accident.

nuggets.text: The 8:30 slot on Tuesdays and Wednesdays is the one Casa Verde can't fill.
nuggets.quote: The eight-thirty slot is the hard one, that's the one I can't fill on Tuesday and Wednesday.

nuggets.text: Lucia wants a waitlist that texts people when a table opens; her Saturday paper waitlist goes unused because she forgets it.
nuggets.quote: A waitlist that texts people when a table opens. I have a paper list on Saturdays and it never gets used because I forget.

nuggets.text: One double-booking plus one no-show table costs $300–400 per bad weekend, so the $79 fee matters less than a reliable Saturday.
nuggets.quote: I'd say each bad weekend, one double-booking and one no-show table, that's three hundred, four hundred dollars. So seventy-nine a month, it's not about the price. It's about the Saturday.

nuggets.text: About 70% of supper bookings arrive by WhatsApp, the rest by phone or walk-in, all written into a hardback paper book.
nuggets.quote: WhatsApp, mostly. Maybe seventy percent. The rest phone, a few walk in and ask. I have a paper book.

nuggets.text: Tomasz answers each WhatsApp request and then copies the booking into the paper book by hand.
nuggets.quote: People write "table for four Friday?" and I write back yes or no and then I copy it into the book. By hand.

nuggets.text: Handling bookings takes Tomasz only 10–15 minutes in the morning plus some in the evening, and he doesn't see it as a big job.
nuggets.quote: Maybe ten, fifteen minutes in the morning and some in the evening. It's not a big job.

nuggets.text: Tomasz once wrote a Friday booking on the Thursday page and 14 people arrived when the book said 6; it happens two or three times a year.
nuggets.quote: Because I once wrote Friday in the Thursday page. Fourteen people turned up and the book said six. That was a bad night.

nuggets.text: With 2–3 supper no-shows a month out of ~90 (about 3%), Tomasz won't build a system around no-shows.
nuggets.quote: The food is already cooked for them, it hurts, but I'm not going to build a whole system around three percent.

nuggets.text: Tomasz sends a same-day WhatsApp reminder to each supper guest (about five minutes) and calls those who don't reply.
nuggets.quote: I write them on the day. "See you tonight at seven, yes?" In WhatsApp. It takes me five minutes and most reply with a thumbs-up. The ones who don't reply, I call.

nuggets.text: Tomasz thinks an automated reminder text would feel cold for a friendly café; guests like a human message.
nuggets.quote: People like a human message. I think a robot text would feel cold for a place like ours.

nuggets.text: Tomasz cancelled a SeatNow free trial the day before it converted because $49/month equals twelve sourdough loaves a week just for a calendar.
nuggets.quote: But then they wanted forty-nine dollars a month and I thought, forty-nine dollars, that's twelve loaves of my sourdough sold at full price, every week, just to have a calendar.

nuggets.text: Tomasz would consider about $15 a month, $20 at most, if it fixed the wrong-page problem.
nuggets.quote: For what I do, like, fifteen dollars, I would think about it. Twenty, at most.

nuggets.text: SeatNow asked Tomasz to draw a floor plan and set up turn times and zones for what is one long table.
nuggets.quote: Too many buttons. It wanted me to draw my floor plan, set up the "turn times," the "zones." I have a long table. One table.

nuggets.text: Tomasz won't pay for SMS reminders because WhatsApp is free and every guest has it.
nuggets.quote: WhatsApp is free. Everybody has it. I write to them there, they write back there. Why would I pay for a text message?

nuggets.text: Tomasz believes asking for a $20 deposit would send half his guests to another café.
nuggets.quote: If I say "send me twenty dollars before you come," half of them go to the other café.

nuggets.text: A deposit feels like asking guests to prove they're not criminals; Tomasz would rather lose 3% than lose the mood.
nuggets.quote: Asking for a deposit, it's like asking them to prove they're not criminals. I'd rather lose three percent than lose the mood.

nuggets.text: For the $35 Christmas set-menu supper, which books out, Tomasz has considered a small deposit.
nuggets.quote: I thought about it for the Christmas supper, because that one is thirty-five dollar set menu and it books out. Maybe for that one, a small amount.

nuggets.text: Collecting a deposit is too much trouble because Tomasz only has a Square card reader.
nuggets.quote: But then I'd have to collect it, and I don't have a card machine that does that, I have the Square reader and that's it. So it's too much trouble.

nuggets.text: Tomasz wants to turn a WhatsApp message into a calendar booking with one button and see the days at a glance.
nuggets.quote: If a person writes to me, I press one button, it goes in a calendar, and it shows me the days.

nuggets.text: The tool must not make him draw anything or show twenty-option screens; if he needs a tutorial, he's out.
nuggets.quote: And it must not make me draw anything. And no screen with twenty options. If I need a tutorial, I'm out.

nuggets.text: Tomasz wants a warning when more than 22 people are booked on one evening.
nuggets.quote: And maybe it warns me if I put more than twenty-two people on one evening.

nuggets.text: Tomasz says his customers won't download an app; a link with a three-question form (name, party size, day) is enough.
nuggets.quote: My customers are not downloading an app to book a flat white and a supper. A link, a form, three questions. Name, how many, what day.

nuggets.text: Guests like free-form messages such as asking for a window table for a stroller, which a booking form can't capture.
nuggets.quote: It's the free-form that people like. They write whatever they want, "we have a stroller, can we have the window?" You can't do that with a form.

nuggets.text: Older guests phone, younger guests use WhatsApp or Instagram, and almost nobody asks for website booking.
nuggets.quote: The older ones phone. The younger ones WhatsApp, or Instagram. Nobody, almost nobody, asks for a website booking.

nuggets.text: The paper book keeps working through power cuts and Wi-Fi outages (twice last winter), which software can't promise.
nuggets.quote: When there's a power cut or the Wi-Fi goes, which happens, I still have my book. That is a big plus. Software dies, paper doesn't.

nuggets.text: Tomasz would try a free tool for a month but expects to drift back to the paper book because the pen is faster.
nuggets.quote: A free one, sure. I'd try it for a month. I can't promise I'd keep using it. I tend to go back to the book. The pen is faster.

nuggets.text: Tomasz doesn't want customers' phone numbers in an unknown cloud after reading about a booking-company data leak.
nuggets.quote: I don't want my customers' phone numbers in somebody's cloud I don't know.

nuggets.text: Tomasz's single wish is to never again write a Friday booking on the Thursday page.
nuggets.quote: Never again write Friday on the Thursday page.

nuggets.text: About 85% of Sunny Side's 140–150 Saturday covers are walk-ins, so the host's main job is the queue, not reservations.
nuggets.quote: On Saturday we do around a hundred and forty, a hundred and fifty covers, Sunday is similar. And probably eighty-five percent are people without a booking. They just walk in.

nuggets.text: The host writes walk-ins on a clipboard sheet and shouts names to about 50 people waiting on the street.
nuggets.quote: We write people down on a sheet on a clipboard, well, the kind with a clip. Name, how many people, phone number if they give it. Then I go out onto the street and shout: "Olena, four!" And there are fifty people standing on the street, all looking at me.

nuggets.text: At 11:30 on Saturday 13–15 groups wait 40–60 minutes; Oksana quotes 20 minutes so they don't leave, and they end up angry.
nuggets.quote: They wait forty minutes, an hour. I say "twenty minutes", because otherwise they'll leave, and then it's forty. And they're angry.

nuggets.text: The worst part is that called guests have often left for another café or gone home without the host knowing.
nuggets.quote: The worst thing is that people leave and I don't know. I go out, shout the name, and they're not there. They've gone for coffee at the café next door, or home altogether.

nuggets.text: A table waits empty 3–7 minutes for a party that left, 10–12 times a shift, almost an hour of lost table time.
nuggets.quote: Three to five minutes, sometimes seven. If you count, there are maybe ten or twelve such cases per shift. That's almost an hour of lost table time.

nuggets.text: Oksana spends about 1–1.5 hours a shift just explaining how much longer the wait will be.
nuggets.quote: Probably an hour, an hour and a half per shift just on explaining how much longer the wait is.

nuggets.text: At peak 4–5 calls an hour ask whether there are free tables, and the answer is always no.
nuggets.quote: They call, they ask "are there free tables?" Four or five calls an hour at peak. I pick up and say "no", and that's it.

nuggets.text: Sunny Side used a free queue tool, QueueBee, for 1–2 months where guests entered their number and got a message, but went back to the clipboard when the owner learned it was paid (about $45/month, reported secondhand).
nuggets.quote: Once we had a free one, it was called "QueueBee", they say. For a month or two. The guest entered their own number there and got a message. It was cool, honestly. But then the owner said it was paid, and we went back to the clipboard.

nuggets.text: With QueueBee guests waited in the square drinking coffee until a 'your table is ready' message, so the host didn't have to shout.
nuggets.quote: I liked that I don't shout on the street. People sit in the little square next door, drink coffee, and they get a message: "Your table is ready". That was super.

nuggets.text: Typing every guest into the tablet herself took too long with busy hands; Oksana needs guests to sign themselves up.
nuggets.quote: What I didn't like was that entering took too long, well, I had to write everyone into the system on the tablet myself, and my hands are busy. I need the guest to sign themselves up.

nuggets.text: Oksana wants a QR code on the door where guests enter name, party size and number and appear on her list.
nuggets.quote: Yes! A QR code, you scan, write your name, how many of you, the number, and that's it. And I see the list.

nuggets.text: Oksana doesn't want an app; only about one guest in twenty has asked for one, the rest just scan with the camera.
nuggets.quote: I don't want any app. One guest once asked us "where's the app?", but I think that's one in twenty. Everyone just turns on the camera and scans.

nuggets.text: Table-ready messages should be SMS, not a messenger, because weekend tourists may not have the café's messenger.
nuggets.quote: SMS. Not a messenger, because not everyone has one. Because tourists, those who came for the weekend, may not have our messenger, but everyone has SMS.

nuggets.text: The table-ready message should say the table is held for five minutes, after which the party loses its place or goes to the end.
nuggets.quote: And it should say the table is held for five minutes. After that they lose their place in the queue, or go to the end.

nuggets.text: At 5 cents an SMS versus a ~$40 table check, one saved empty table pays for it; Oksana would pay per message rather than per month.
nuggets.quote: If an SMS costs five cents, and a table standing empty for five minutes is, well, an average check of forty dollars per table for forty minutes, then it pays for itself in one go. It's a trifle. I'd pay per message, not per month.

nuggets.text: A 500-message monthly cap is too low for ~70 groups a day on weekends (about 400 per weekend); Sunny Side needs at least 2,000.
nuggets.quote: A limit of five hundred messages a month is too little, because on weekends we do seventy groups a day, that's already four hundred per weekend. I need at least two thousand.

nuggets.text: Oksana guesses a texted waitlist would roughly halve empty-table cases from 10–12 to about 5 per shift, but says it is a guess.
nuggets.quote: I think about half. From ten or twelve cases down to five. But that's my guess.

nuggets.text: A booked birthday table for eight didn't show or call on a Saturday at 10:30, after the host had set it up with balloons.
nuggets.quote: We once prepared a table for eight, for a birthday, and they didn't come, and didn't call.

nuggets.text: Oksana supports a $20-per-person deposit for groups of eight or more but not for couples or threes at brunch.
nuggets.quote: For big groups, say from eight, why not. Twenty dollars per person, and if you don't come, you lose it. But for ordinary people, for two or three, no, it's brunch.

nuggets.text: According to the host, Sunny Side's owner would want a deposit for everyone, but he doesn't stand at the door.
nuggets.quote: Well, the owner, I think, would want a deposit for everyone, but he doesn't stand at the door.

nuggets.text: Servers don't tell the host when a table is cleared, so she keeps asking from outside and seats late.
nuggets.quote: The waiters don't say when a table has been freed. They may have already cleared it, but I don't know, because I'm outside.

nuggets.text: Oksana wants green/yellow/red table status on the tablet plus a signal when guests ask for the bill, meaning a table in about ten minutes.
nuggets.quote: Yes, three colours. Green, yellow, red. I'd also like to see when guests have asked for the bill. Then I know there'll be a table in ten minutes.

nuggets.text: Oksana wants a screen outside showing how many groups are ahead, because she answers 'how's it going?' about 40 times a shift.
nuggets.quote: Well, I'm thinking about a kind of screen outside. So people can see how many groups are still ahead of them. Then they don't ask me every five minutes "so how's it going?".

nuggets.text: Oksana loved the idea of a guest link showing queue position with a cancel option, so she stops calling names into the void.
nuggets.quote: Great. Very. Because then I'm not shouting "Olena!" into the void. If she cancelled, I see it. That's exactly the main thing.

nuggets.text: Buttons must be big because the host often works with sauce on her hands or in gloves.
nuggets.quote: Except maybe tell your developers that my hands are in sauce, so the buttons have to be big.

nuggets.text: Harbor & Pine's owner pays about $129/month for SeatNow and has used it for three years.
nuggets.quote: SeatNow. The owner pays for it, I think it's a hundred and twenty-nine a month for our size, don't quote me.

nuggets.text: SeatNow's table view shows the whole floor: who's seated, on dessert or has asked for the check.
nuggets.quote: The table management is solid. I can see the whole floor, who's seated, who's on dessert, who's asked for the check.

nuggets.text: SMS reminders cut Harbor & Pine's no-shows from about 12% to 6–7%.
nuggets.quote: Before SMS reminders our no-shows were around twelve percent. Now it's more like six, seven.

nuggets.text: Devon pays about 4 cents a text and would pay double, since halved no-shows are worth ~$700 a weekend night.
nuggets.quote: They charge us, I think, like four cents a text. Whatever. I'd pay double.

nuggets.text: Late cancellations, such as 5:30 for a 7:00 booking, remain the top problem even with reminders.
nuggets.quote: The reminder helps, but the people who cancel at five-thirty for a seven o'clock, that's the thing.

nuggets.text: Devon spends about 1.5 hours every Sunday building the schedule in a Google Sheet and gets it wrong about once a week, at ~$140 per server shift.
nuggets.quote: It takes me maybe an hour and a half every Sunday, and I get it wrong about once a week.

nuggets.text: Devon wants a staffing recommendation, or at least a forecast of covers by hour, from bookings and history.
nuggets.quote: It's a guess either way but I'd love a recommendation. Even just a forecast of covers by hour.

nuggets.text: Walk-ins (15–20% on weekends) aren't logged; the host keeps tally marks on a clipboard.
nuggets.quote: I don't log them anywhere, my host does a tally mark on a clipboard.

nuggets.text: Devon wants a big 'add walk-in, party of two' button that takes two taps.
nuggets.quote: Yeah, a big button. "Add walk-in, party of two." Two taps.

nuggets.text: A $10-per-head deposit on Friday/Saturday 7–9pm bookings, refundable up to 24 hours before, cut no-shows in those slots from 8% to under 2%.
nuggets.quote: The no-show rate in those slots went from eight percent to under two.

nuggets.text: Guests' deposit complaints (about one a week) are mostly about not wanting to enter a card; one left a one-star review.
nuggets.quote: Mostly "I don't want to put my card in." Some said "we're a restaurant, not a concert." One guy left a one-star review about it.

nuggets.text: Devon believes a non-refundable deposit loses a chunk of guests, while refundable-until-a-day-before just signals the restaurant is serious.
nuggets.quote: If it's non-refundable, I think you lose a chunk of people. Refundable until a day before, it just says "we're serious."

nuggets.text: Harbor & Pine charges deposits only for prime slots and parties of six or more, never early seatings or Tuesdays.
nuggets.quote: Only prime slots. And for parties of six-plus, any day. Not for early seating or Tuesday. You don't want to scare people when you need them.

nuggets.text: About 30 calls a day at 2–3 minutes each cost about 1.5 hours of host time, and 5–6 calls a night go to voicemail.
nuggets.quote: We get about thirty calls a day, and each takes two or three minutes.

nuggets.text: Devon wants the phone line to offer 'press one for a text with a booking link'.
nuggets.quote: Like if the phone just said "press one for a text with a booking link." Yes.

nuggets.text: Letting guests log in to change party size or cancel would cut calls to the host stand.
nuggets.quote: If they had a thing where they could log in and edit, add a person, cancel, I'd get fewer calls.

nuggets.text: Devon thinks a guest app feels more 'official' than a link, especially for younger guests who live on their phones.
nuggets.quote: A link in the text can do it too, but I think an app feels more "official." Younger guests, they live on their phone.

nuggets.text: Forced to pick, Devon would prioritise the link because there's no download, but would test an app because it may drive bookings weeks out.
nuggets.quote: If I had to pick one, the link. Because no download. But, I don't know, the thing I've seen at the bigger places is that an app gets people to book weeks out. I'd test it.

nuggets.text: Allergies, anniversaries and high-chair requests share one free-text notes blob and the host misses them.
nuggets.quote: We write "shellfish allergy" and "celebrating anniversary" and "high chair" all in one blob and the host misses it.

nuggets.text: Devon wants structured tags (allergy, high chair, wheelchair, birthday) with allergies shown on the kitchen ticket.
nuggets.quote: I'd love tags. Allergy, high chair, wheelchair, birthday. Structured, so the kitchen sees the allergy on the ticket.

nuggets.text: Harbor & Pine overbooks the 7:30 slot by two covers on ~7% expected no-shows, which backfired twice last summer.
nuggets.quote: We overbook, a little. Like by two covers during the seven-thirty slot, because we know about seven percent won't show.

nuggets.text: Devon wants the tool to suggest how much to overbook based on history instead of guessing.
nuggets.quote: I want the tool to do it, suggest how much to overbook based on history. A smart overbooking. Right now I'm guessing.

nuggets.text: No-show prediction plus a staffing forecast would be worth another $50/month to the owner, since one saved server shift a week is $400–500 a month.
nuggets.quote: Honestly if the thing gave me no-show prediction and the staffing forecast, I'd tell the owner it's worth another fifty a month.

nuggets.text: Switching from SeatNow would require convincing an owner who doesn't like change.
nuggets.quote: I'd have to convince the owner and the owner doesn't like change.

nuggets.text: A host with a ringing phone and a line has three seconds; anything over two taps won't be used.
nuggets.quote: A host with a ringing phone and a line at the door has three seconds. If a thing takes more than two taps, it won't be used.

nuggets.text: Priya finds places on Instagram, saves them and leaves them for weeks until friends suggest going out.
nuggets.quote: Someone posts a place, I save it, and then it sits in my saved folder for three weeks until somebody says "should we go somewhere Friday?"

nuggets.text: Priya refuses to phone; if a place requires a call she picks a different place.
nuggets.quote: If a place makes me call, I'll pick a different place.

nuggets.text: This happens about twice a month, and Priya says none of her friends under ~35 call either.
nuggets.quote: Out of ten I'd say that happens maybe twice a month. And I'm not unusual, all my friends are the same. Nobody under, like, thirty-five calls.

nuggets.text: Instead of calling, Priya DMs the restaurant on Instagram and waits for a reply.
nuggets.quote: I send an Instagram message: "Hi, do you have a table for four on Saturday around eight?" And then I wait.

nuggets.text: When a DM reply comes the next afternoon, Priya has already booked elsewhere or the group has lost interest; she waits an hour at most.
nuggets.quote: Sometimes it's the next afternoon, and by then I've booked somewhere else, or my friends have lost interest.

nuggets.text: DM booking turns into back-and-forth about times and ends with her sharing her phone number in a DM, which she dislikes.
nuggets.quote: And I'm giving them my phone number in a DM, which I don't love.

nuggets.text: After a DM booking Priya got no confirmation and once arrived with four people to find nothing in the book.
nuggets.quote: No confirmation. I just hope. I once showed up and they had nothing in the book. Four of us, standing there.

nuggets.text: Priya just wants a message saying she is booked, with day, time and party size.
nuggets.quote: A confirmation. Like a message that says "You're booked, Saturday, eight, four people." That's literally all.

nuggets.text: The best case is a link in the Instagram bio that books date and time in under a minute, which she has used at three places.
nuggets.quote: Like, the best case is: link in bio, I tap, pick date, pick time, it's done in under a minute.

nuggets.text: Priya won't create an account or download an app to reserve; she'd rather DM.
nuggets.quote: I will not download an app for a restaurant. If it's "download our app to reserve," I'm out. I'd rather DM.

nuggets.text: WhatsApp also works for Priya, but Instagram comes first because that's where she found the place.
nuggets.quote: Or WhatsApp, WhatsApp is also fine. But I'd say Instagram first because that's where I found the place.

nuggets.text: Priya likes day-before and day-of reminders but prefers DM or WhatsApp because she mostly ignores SMS.
nuggets.quote: A text message is fine, but I'd honestly prefer it in DM or WhatsApp. SMS I mostly ignore, my phone's full of delivery codes and spam.

nuggets.text: Priya would confirm with 'reply Y' or a one-tap button, but not if she has to log in.
nuggets.quote: Yes, if it's just "reply Y to confirm" or a one-tap button. I'd do that. But not if I have to log in.

nuggets.text: Priya paid a $110-per-person deposit for a tasting menu, refundable until 48 hours before, and was fine with it because it was special.
nuggets.quote: Once, for a tasting menu, a hundred and ten dollars each. It was charged to my card and refundable until forty-eight hours before. That I was okay with, because it's a special thing.

nuggets.text: A $20 deposit for a table of four on an ordinary Saturday would make Priya close the tab and book elsewhere; it feels like distrust.
nuggets.quote: If a place asked me for a twenty-dollar deposit for a table of four on a random Saturday, I'd close the tab and go somewhere else.

nuggets.text: Even refundable, Priya doesn't want to enter her card for a place she hasn't tried, unless the table is booked up for a month.
nuggets.quote: I don't want to put my card in a form for a place I haven't tried.

nuggets.text: A no-show fee charged afterwards feels fairer to Priya than prepaying, as long as she is warned.
nuggets.quote: That feels more fair than prepaying. But I'd want a warning.

nuggets.text: Arriving on time and waiting 20 minutes with no explanation annoys Priya; even 'ten more minutes' or a text would help.
nuggets.quote: When I arrive on time and then wait twenty minutes with no explanation. Even "table's almost ready, ten minutes" would help.

nuggets.text: At a ramen place Priya scanned a QR code, saw she was number seven, went for a walk and got a text, and wants that everywhere.
nuggets.quote: You scan a code at the door, it shows you're number seven, and then you go for a walk. That was awesome.

nuggets.text: Priya would never pay to join a queue and says guests shouldn't be charged for basics.
nuggets.quote: No. I'd never pay to join a queue.

nuggets.text: Priya cancels by message and feels guilty; she would use a 'cancel booking' link in the confirmation immediately.
nuggets.quote: If there was a link in my confirmation, "cancel booking," I'd use it so fast. Less awkward than texting.

nuggets.text: Being remembered is a nice bonus but Priya wouldn't choose a restaurant for it.
nuggets.quote: It's more like a bonus. I wouldn't choose a place for that.

nuggets.text: Priya wants the booking link where she already looks: Instagram bio, Google listing and the DM auto-reply.
nuggets.quote: Put the booking link where I'm already looking. In the Instagram bio, in the Google listing, in the DM auto-reply.

nuggets.text: Marcus has dinner out about eight times a month and spends around $70 a head with wine.
nuggets.quote: I probably spend around seventy dollars a head on dinner, with wine.

nuggets.text: Marcus rotates three regular restaurants and has been to the Italian 40–50 times over four years.
nuggets.quote: I have three that I rotate.

nuggets.text: Marcus keeps going back because the staff know his table, his wine and his partner's nut allergy without being told.
nuggets.quote: Because they know me. That's the whole thing.

nuggets.text: The tapas place's manager sent a free birthday plate after seeing the date in their system, unprompted.
nuggets.quote: the manager once sent out a free plate for my birthday. I hadn't even mentioned it, they just saw it in their system.

nuggets.text: After about 30 visits the Japanese counter still asks Marcus whether he has been there before.
nuggets.quote: After thirty visits, I'm a stranger there. Every time I book they ask "have you been here before?"

nuggets.text: Feeling invisible, Marcus cut visits to the Japanese place from monthly to every three months without telling them.
nuggets.quote: I used to go there monthly, now it's every three months. I never told them why. People don't complain, they just drift.

nuggets.text: Marcus wants to log in once and record his partner's allergy so every booking carries it.
nuggets.quote: If I could log in somewhere and say, "Hey, my partner's allergy, here it is," then they'd have it for every booking, and I'd never repeat it.

nuggets.text: Repeating his partner's nut allergy to every restaurant, every time, is exhausting and a little scary.
nuggets.quote: I repeat the allergy thing every single time, to every restaurant, it's exhausting and a little scary.

nuggets.text: Marcus would like one app holding all his bookings and one profile across his three restaurants, not an app per restaurant.
nuggets.quote: Not an app per restaurant, one that has all my bookings.

nuggets.text: A link is perfect for a place visited twice a year, but for forty visits Marcus wants an app or at least an account.
nuggets.quote: If you go twice a year, a link is perfect. If you go forty times, give me an app. Or an account at least.

nuggets.text: Marcus uses one big booking platform app for upscale places, but it doesn't list his local independents.
nuggets.quote: I already use one big platform app for, you know, the fancy ones, and it's fine, but it doesn't have my little local places.

nuggets.text: Marcus books his Italian by texting the owner directly, the tapas place through its website widget and the Japanese counter by phone.
nuggets.quote: The Italian, I text the owner. Directly.

nuggets.text: After 30-plus bookings the tapas widget still makes Marcus type his name, email and phone every time.
nuggets.quote: Why am I typing my phone number? I'd like it to remember.

nuggets.text: The widget has no table-preference field, so Marcus writes it in notes and doesn't know if anyone reads them.
nuggets.quote: I have to add it in the notes, and I don't know if anyone reads the notes.

nuggets.text: Marcus reads his texts and likes an SMS reminder with 'reply 1 to confirm, 2 to cancel'.
nuggets.quote: I'm perfectly happy with SMS. I read my texts. A text with "Reply 1 to confirm, 2 to cancel", that's perfect for me.

nuggets.text: Marcus has no problem with a ~$20-per-head deposit on Friday or Saturday prime slots if it comes off the bill.
nuggets.quote: For a Friday or Saturday prime slot, absolutely, no problem.

nuggets.text: Deposits should be waived for known regulars like him and asked of strangers booking eight seats on a Saturday.
nuggets.quote: If I'm someone who's come forty times, don't ask me for a card. Ask the stranger who just booked eight seats on a Saturday.

nuggets.text: Marcus accepts a no-show fee only if clearly agreed at booking; an unseen $50 charge he would dispute with his card company.
nuggets.quote: Some places do it sneakily, that's what I hate. A fifty-dollar charge I'd not seen. That I would dispute with my card company.

nuggets.text: Marcus would pay $4–5 a month, no more, for guaranteed priority tables at his three places on busy nights.
nuggets.quote: If an app really gave me priority at my three places, like a guaranteed table on a busy night, I'd pay a few dollars a month. Four, five dollars. Not more.

nuggets.text: Marcus finds paying to be a regular weird; recognition should feel earned.
nuggets.quote: It's weird to pay to be a regular. It should feel earned.

nuggets.text: Points and punch cards don't motivate Marcus; he values recognition over discounts.
nuggets.quote: Honestly, points don't excite me. I'm not buying dinner to get a free coffee. What I like is not a discount, it's recognition.

nuggets.text: Regulars' knowledge lives in the 62-year-old owner's head and is lost when staff change; a system would keep it.
nuggets.quote: If it were in a system, it would stay. That's the point.

nuggets.text: When booking for his partner's birthday, Marcus wants the note to actually reach the table.
nuggets.quote: When I book for my partner's birthday, I'd love to add a note and have it actually reach the table.

nuggets.text: Marcus says remembering his partner's allergy alone is something he would pay for.
nuggets.quote: Remember my partner's allergy so I don't have to say it out loud. That alone I'd pay for, honestly.
